notes:
Task and constraints: Determine whether at most one element can be changed to make nums non-decreasing.
Idea: Scan adjacent values and track whether a descending pair has already been repaired.
Technique and why it applies: At a descent, the code logically lowers the previous value by updating prev to nums[i] when the element two positions back allows it. Otherwise the commented-out alternative would raise the current value, but that branch is disabled.
Invariant: prev represents the effective previous value after the single allowed adjustment, and modified records whether a descent has occurred.
Edge cases: Empty nums causes nums[0] to fail; the usual problem has at least one value. Because the else repair branch is commented out, cases requiring raising nums[i] can be classified incorrectly.
Complexity: The scan is O(n) time and O(1) space, but the disabled branch makes the implementation's correctness incomplete. Author labels describe the intended algorithm.

Task and constraints: Construct a permutation of 1 through n with exactly k distinct absolute differences between adjacent elements.
Idea: Start with a consecutive increasing prefix, then append values using alternating positive and negative steps of decreasing size.
Technique and why it applies: The prefix creates difference one. The alternating steps generate the distinct differences k,k-1,...,1 while remaining within the allowed value range.
Invariant: res is a valid prefix of the permutation, and each alternating step adds a new adjacent difference not used earlier.
Edge cases: The standard constraints require 1<=k<n. The loop appends k values after n-k initial values, producing exactly n values.
Complexity: Building the prefix and appending k values takes O(n) time and O(n) output space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Build a permutation of 1..n with exactly k distinct neighboring absolute differences.
Idea: Alternate choosing the smallest remaining number and largest remaining number while decreasing k toward one.
Technique and why it applies: Each switch between the low and high ends introduces a new large difference; after k reaches one, remaining choices proceed from one side and add only difference one.
Invariant: result contains each chosen endpoint exactly once, while left and right delimit unused values.
Edge cases: The loop always emits n values. It assumes the input k lies in the problem's valid range; k=0 would produce an ordinary descending sequence but is outside usual constraints.
Complexity: Every value is appended once, so time is O(n) and output storage is O(n). The author O(1) space label omits the result list.

Task and constraints: Find the kth smallest value in an m-by-n multiplication table.
Idea: Binary-search the value range and count how many table entries are no greater than each midpoint.
Technique and why it applies: For each row i, the number of entries at most x is min(x//i,n). If the total count is below k, the answer is larger; otherwise the upper bound is reduced.
Invariant: L and R bound the smallest value whose count is at least k, and ans stores the best feasible midpoint found.
Edge cases: The table values begin at one, but L starts at zero, which is a harmless extra search point. The supplied indentation in the count helper comments is irregular.
Complexity: Each count costs O(m); binary search over values up to mn takes O(log(mn)) rounds, so time is O(m log(mn)) and space O(1). No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Maximize an integer by swapping at most two digits once.
Idea: Scan digits from right to left, remember the largest digit seen, and record a swap whenever that digit exceeds the current digit.
Technique and why it applies: The rightmost occurrence of the maximum digit is preferred because swapping it into an earlier position creates the largest possible number. The last recorded pair corresponds to the leftmost position that can improve.
Invariant: max_idx identifies the largest digit in the suffix scanned so far; left and right record the most significant beneficial swap candidate.
Edge cases: If digits are already non-increasing from left to right, left and right remain zero and swapping the first digit with itself leaves the number unchanged. The code handles no-swap cases implicitly.
Complexity: Converting and scanning d digits takes O(d) time and O(d) space. The author space label is consistent with digit-list storage.

Task and constraints: Count distinct bulb configurations reachable after exactly m button presses, with four periodic toggle operations.
Idea: Reduce n to at most three bulbs and return precomputed counts based on n and m.
Technique and why it applies: Bulbs beyond the first three repeat the same toggle patterns as earlier bulbs, and applying a button pattern more than three times adds no new configuration. The small case table gives the known reachable-state counts.
Invariant: The answer depends only on min(n,3) and whether m is zero, one, two, or at least three.
Edge cases: The code indexes n-1 after clamping n, so it assumes n>=1. m=0 returns the single unchanged configuration.
Complexity: A few constant-time branches yield O(1) time and O(1) auxiliary space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Count distinct states of n bulbs after m presses of the available toggle buttons.
Idea: Use the finite set of possible outcomes for the small cases and return the appropriate count through conditionals.
Technique and why it applies: The number of distinguishable bulb patterns stabilizes once n is at least three and m is sufficiently large. The conditions encode these known cases directly rather than simulating every button sequence.
Invariant: Each branch returns the count for a disjoint parameter case determined by n and m.
Edge cases: m=0 returns one unchanged state; n=1 always has two states when m>0. The branch order handles n=2 and m=1 before the broader cases.
Complexity: The method uses a fixed number of comparisons and returns, so time and space are O(1), matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Count how many longest strictly increasing subsequences exist in nums.
Idea: Maintain lists by subsequence length, storing candidate ending values with counts, and use binary search to choose a level for each new value.
Technique and why it applies: A new value may extend a shorter subsequence or replace an ending candidate at a suitable length. Counts from smaller ending values are summed to count ways to reach the current value.
Invariant: sub_list[length-1] stores candidate tails and counts for increasing subsequences of that length.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero. The count aggregation and tail replacement logic is nonstandard and may not correctly preserve all LIS counts for duplicates or multiple candidate tails; correctness needs verification.
Complexity: Binary search is O(log n), but rebuilding cur_sub and summing prior-level candidates can cost O(n) per element, giving O(n²) time and O(n²) storage in the worst case. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Count the number of longest strictly increasing subsequences in nums.
Idea: For each index, store the longest subsequence length ending there and the number of ways to achieve that length.
Technique and why it applies: Every earlier smaller value can extend its subsequences. If it produces an equal best length, counts are added; if it produces a longer one, the current state is replaced. The global result sums counts at the maximum length.
Invariant: dp[i] is [best length ending at i, number of subsequences of that length].
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero because result and max_len remain zero. Equal values cannot extend a strictly increasing subsequence because the comparison uses >.
Complexity: The nested loops take O(n²) time and the DP list uses O(n) space, matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Find the length of the longest strictly increasing contiguous run in nums.
Idea: Start a run at every index and extend it until the next value is not greater than the previous value.
Technique and why it applies: The inner loop follows adjacent values while each next number exceeds the last accepted number. The longest run found from any start is the answer.
Invariant: c is the length of the strictly increasing contiguous run beginning at i.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero because the outer loop does not execute. A single value yields one. The algorithm repeatedly scans overlapping runs.
Complexity: Worst-case time is O(n²) for an already increasing array, with O(1) auxiliary space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Return the longest strictly increasing contiguous subsequence length.
Idea: Track the current increasing run and update the maximum whenever the next value exceeds the previous one.
Technique and why it applies: A strict increase extends the run; otherwise the current run resets to one starting at the current element. result records the longest run encountered.
Invariant: count is the length of the increasing run ending at index i, and result is the maximum so far.
Edge cases: Empty input returns zero because the loop is skipped. Equal adjacent values reset the run because the comparison is strictly less than.
Complexity: One pass gives O(n) time and O(1) auxiliary space, matching author labels.

Task and constraints: Cut all trees in increasing height order, moving through a grid where zero cells are blocked, and return the total steps.
Idea: Collect and sort tree heights, then run BFS from the current position to each next tree.
Technique and why it applies: BFS computes the shortest path through walkable cells. The current location is updated as the search reaches each target tree, and the distances are accumulated.
Invariant: Before each target, (ux,uy) is the previous tree location and dist stores shortest distances from that start.
Edge cases: If a tree cannot be reached, return -1. The code assumes forest is nonempty. It sorts heights but not positions; equal-height trees are processed by height only, which is sufficient if equal-height order does not affect the minimum total.
Complexity: For T trees and an m-by-n grid, each BFS is O(mn), giving O(Tmn) time and O(mn) distance/queue space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Find the minimum walking distance needed to cut every tree in increasing height order.
Idea: Sort trees in a min-heap and run BFS separately from the current position to each tree.
Technique and why it applies: minStep explores four-neighbor walkable cells level by level and returns the first distance to the target. The outer loop adds this shortest distance and advances the start to that tree.
Invariant: The heap yields trees in increasing height, and start is the position of the last tree cut.
Edge cases: Unreachable trees return -1. The helper closes over m and n, which are defined before it is called. The approach repeatedly scans the grid, explaining the TLE label for many trees.
Complexity: Each BFS costs O(mn), repeated for T trees, so time is O(Tmn) and memory O(mn) for the queue and visited set. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Cut all trees in ascending height order while minimizing walking distance through nonzero cells.
Idea: Sort trees by height and use a custom closer/detour frontier search to estimate shortest paths between successive trees.
Technique and why it applies: The dot product classifies neighbors as moving toward or away from the target. When the closer frontier empties, the method expands detour nodes while increasing the estimated path length by two.
Invariant: min_steps is the current estimated path length; closer and detour hold candidate cells grouped by whether they move toward the target.
Edge cases: The heuristic search is nonstandard and should not be assumed to guarantee shortest paths without proof. Blocked or unreachable targets return -1 when both frontiers empty.
Complexity: In the worst case the search can visit O(mn) cells per tree, giving O(Tmn) time and O(mn) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Determine whether a string of parentheses and '*' can be valid when each '*' represents '(', ')', or empty.
Idea: Store unmatched left parentheses, unmatched right parentheses, and star positions, then use stars to repair unmatched symbols.
Technique and why it applies: Initial matching pairs left parentheses with later right parentheses. Remaining stars must occur after unmatched left parentheses to close them and before unmatched right parentheses to open them.
Invariant: The three deques contain indices of unmatched left/right symbols and available stars in ascending order.
Edge cases: Empty input should be valid, but the code accesses deque without importing it. The final loop returns True once both unmatched lists empty, but if stars run out while one list remains it may fall through without an explicit False return, yielding None.
Complexity: The scans and deque operations are O(n) time and O(n) space. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Validate parentheses where each '*' can act as an opening parenthesis, closing parenthesis, or empty string.
Idea: Track lower and upper bounds on the possible number of unmatched opening parentheses while scanning.
Technique and why it applies: '(' increases both bounds, ')' decreases both, and '*' decreases the lower bound while increasing the range of possible interpretations by decreasing upper. If upper becomes negative, no interpretation is valid; lower is clamped to zero.
Invariant: lower and upper bound the feasible unmatched-open count after the processed prefix.
Edge cases: An early negative upper bound breaks the loop and the final lower==0 check then may incorrectly return True because it does not explicitly remember the failure. This is a correctness issue in the shown code.
Complexity: The scan uses O(n) time and O(1) space. Author labels describe the intended algorithm, but the early-break handling is suspect.

Task and constraints: Determine whether four numbers can be combined with arithmetic operations and parentheses to produce 24.
Idea: Recursively choose two numbers, replace them with each possible arithmetic result, and test the reduced list.
Technique and why it applies: Each operation reduces the number of values by one. The recursion tries addition, both subtraction orders, multiplication, and valid divisions, accepting a final value within a small floating tolerance of 24.
Invariant: At each recursive level, nums contains the values remaining after applying operations to selected cards.
Edge cases: Division by zero is skipped. The method mutates nums during branches and restores the selected entries after unsuccessful paths; successful early returns do not restore, but the top-level call ends immediately.
Complexity: The search explores a constant set of operations for each pair, producing exponential/factorial-scale work for the fixed four-card input. Recursion uses O(1) depth under that fixed size. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Check whether four card values can be combined to make exactly 24 using arithmetic operations.
Idea: Recursively combine ordered pairs of numbers with addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division until one value remains.
Technique and why it applies: Each chosen pair is replaced by its result, and recursion explores the remaining expression possibilities. Commutative operations skip duplicate orderings; division by zero is excluded.
Invariant: nums at each call represents the remaining intermediate values after previous operations.
Edge cases: The Fraction import is unused and the implementation uses ordinary arithmetic. The comprehension `i != k != j` is a chained comparison, not the intended `i != k and k != j`, so it can retain or omit the wrong values and compromise correctness.
Complexity: The recursion has factorial-scale branching for the fixed four inputs; temporary lists use O(n) space per depth. No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Determine whether s can become a palindrome after deleting at most one character.
Idea: Recursively compare the outer characters; at the first mismatch, try deleting either the left or right character once.
Technique and why it applies: Matching endpoints can be discarded together. A mismatch allows two possible repairs, but has_deleted prevents any second deletion from being accepted.
Invariant: compare(s,has_deleted) returns whether the current substring can be palindromic within the remaining deletion budget.
Edge cases: Strings of length zero or one are valid. Slicing creates new strings at each recursive call, and the branching happens only at the first mismatch along each path.
Complexity: In the worst case, repeated slicing and recursive comparisons can take O(n²) time and O(n²) cumulative allocation; recursion depth is O(n). No labels were supplied.

Task and constraints: Check whether a string is a palindrome after deleting at most one character.
Idea: Compare from both ends and, at the first mismatch, test the two substrings formed by deleting either endpoint.
Technique and why it applies: If all mirrored characters match, the string is already a palindrome. Otherwise, only one deletion remains, so the helper validates the interior after skipping left or right.
Invariant: left and right delimit the unresolved substring whose outer characters have matched so far.
Edge cases: Empty and single-character strings return True. At most two helper scans are launched, each stopping at its first mismatch.
Complexity: The two-pointer scan and at most two validations take O(n) time, with O(1) auxiliary space. The author labels are correct.
